{"docket_number": "480", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1966", "first_party": "Warden, Maryland Penitentiary", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Bennie Joe Hayden", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit", "argued": ["1967-04-12T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Does the Fourth Amendment create a distinction between merely evidentiary materials, which may not be seized during the course of a search, and the instrumentalities or fruits of the crime, which may be seized?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Around 8 a.m. on March 17, 1962, an armed robber took $363 from the premises of the Diamond Cab Company in Baltimore, Maryland and fled on foot. Two cab drivers were attracted by the yelling and followed the suspect onto Cocoa Lane. One of the cab drivers radioed the company dispatcher a description of the suspect including clothes, which the dispatcher passed on to the police. When the police arrived at the Hayden residence, Mrs. Hayden allowed them to search the house without a warrant. The police found Bennie Joe Hayden in an upstairs bedroom and no one else in the house. They also found a set of clothes matching the description given by the cab driver in the washing machine, as well as a shotgun and a pistol in a flush tank. Ammunition for both weapons was discovered in Hayden’s room.

Hayden was charged with armed robbery and tried in front of a court sitting without a jury. The clothing and the weapons were admitted into evidence at trial without objection, and Hayden was convicted. Hayden sought habeas corpus relief in district court, which was denied. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed the denial of habeas corpus and held that the search was valid but that the clothing had “evidential value only” and was improperly admitted into evidence at trial.

", "conclusion": "

Justice William J. Brennan, Jr. delivered the opinion of the 6-3 majority. The Supreme Court held that the language and purpose of the Fourth Amendment does not support such a distinction. Because the Fourth Amendment was meant to protect the privacy of citizens from being violated by the government, the type of property that is the subject of the search is irrelevant to the protection provided. Justice Hugo L. Black concurred in the judgment.

Justice Abe Fortas wrote a partial concurrence in which he argued that the Fourth Amendment limits the scope of searches to those items which can be directly tied to the commission of a crime. He also argued that the protection against general searches is a fundamental aspect of the Fourth Amendment, and the majority’s opinion damages that protection. Chief Justice Earl Warren joined in the partial concurrence.

In his dissenting opinion, Justice William O. Douglas wrote that the Fourth Amendment provides protection of both privacy and property. He argued that not all evidence discovered in a lawful search is admissible, particularly if it serves a testimonial purpose that would violate the Fifth Amendment rights of the defendant.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 480, Warden, Maryland Penitentiary Petitioner v. Penny Joe Hayden. Mr. Goldstein. Thank you. The motion is granted. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. The facts of this case are relatively undisputed, are quite essential, and may, I think, be briefly stated. Ernest Occинг言. and the dispatcher notified the police. The cab driver in the cab observed the man run into the house and so notified his dispatcher, who again notified the police. The police arrived at the house within minutes of the time that the man had run into the house. After a discussion with the cab driver, the police knocked on the door and Mrs. Benny Jo Hayden opened the door. The police saw no male on the first floor, so one of the officers went to the basement and two others proceeded upstairs. Mr. Benny Jo Hayden was in an upstairs bedroom, feigning sleep, and when no other male was found in the house, he was arrested. Another officer who had come upstairs heard a toilet running in an adjoining bathroom. He went to that bathroom and in the flush tank of the toilet found two guns. What was the last time that the man ran in? According to the record, they arrived at the house within five minutes after the man ran in, which was approximately 15 minutes after the time of the holdup. May I ask what kind of guns they were that they found? One was a pistol with a long barrel, and the other was a sawed-off shotgun. Were either of those guns the type that were used in the murder? Yes, sir. The victim could only say that he felt something very long and hard in his back. He did not see the gun. Nobody really saw the gun at the time of the holdup, but he did say that he felt something long and hard in his back. The officers who were in the room also found ammunition for the guns in a dresser, and they found a sweater and a cap similar to the one described under the mattress. The officer in the basement, while either searching for the man or for the guns or for the money, and the record, frankly, is not totally clear on that, looked into a washing machine, which was in the basement. I should point out here that this was a small three-story row house, not a large house, rather small one, and it was a row house, meaning houses on both sides, and therefore no way out except front or back. He looked into this washing machine and saw a truck driver's uniform with a leather belt still in the pants, and this was similar to the clothing that had been described that was being worn by the person who had committed the felony. The entire search from the time the police entered the house, arrested Mr. Hayden, searched the entire house, took less than an hour. Mr. Hayden was arrested and taken out of the house to the police station within an hour. And this is true even though the money was not found. The items which were found were found almost contemporaneously with the arrest or immediately thereafter. I believe that all the remaining part of the search was engaged in searching for the money. All of the seized items were admitted into evidence without objection by the experienced trial counsel who represented Mr. Hayden at his trial. This counsel did, at trial, very diligently attempt to show that the witnesses, the identifying witnesses, were confused, were confused as to colors. In fact, were confused as to colors of the clothing. I'd now like to consider just briefly how this case reaches this court and give a brief summarization of the litigation. Mr. Hayden was convicted of robbery in the criminal court of Baltimore and was sentenced to 14 years imprisonment. Mr. Hayden did not take a direct appeal and the judge in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland in the original habeas corpus proceeding found that his counsel had advised him of his right to take an appeal. But Mr. Hayden, within the time that he could have taken appeal, did file his first proceeding under the Maryland Post-Conviction Procedure Act, which was denied totally without hearing. An application for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals of Maryland was made and the application was granted. The case was remanded for a full evidentiary hearing. A hearing was held, and the judge in the post-conviction hearing found that the search of the home and the seizure of all the articles was proper. In your state law, you can go right under the state of the head. No, sir, you normally cannot. However, at about this time, there was an extreme interest in the case of Townsend v. Sane of this court, and the Maryland courts made an effort, partly at the prodding of the Attorney General of Maryland, to attempt to have, in our post-conviction proceedings, a full hearing so that when we went into the federal court, we could attempt to rely on the full hearing in the state court. It is also true that Mr. Hayden had claimed, and had originally claimed in the habeas corpus proceeding here, that his counsel had not advised him of his right to appeal. He was certainly unskilled in the law, and though he is very familiar with a number of Supreme Court cases, he is not a lawyer, was not skilled in the law, and claimed that his counsel had not advised him of his right to appeal, and it also claimed incompetency of his trial counsel. Both of these matters were disposed of on the facts in the federal habeas corpus hearing in the district court, but had not been decided at the time of his first post-conviction proceeding and at the time of his first application for leave to appeal. In spite of the fact that Mr. Hayden had been successful in his first application for leave to appeal in the Court of Appeals of Maryland, he filed an application for leave to appeal from the denial of a second application for post-conviction relief, and sometime in the course of that wrote a letter, which is in the record, to withdrawal. We had argued very strenuously in the district court that the withdrawal of his application for leave to appeal, coupled with his refusal to appeal in the first instance, was a deliberate bypass of state proceedings. The district court disagreed with us, and that is not before us at this time. The district court did, however, find, after a full evidentiary hearing, that the arrest was legal as being in hot pursuit, that the search was reasonable, was not exploratory, was within reasonable bounds, and that the seizure of all items was proper. The district court specifically found that the search was much less extensive here, and certainly was not exploratory at all, and was within the bounds of this court's decision in Harris v. United States. Did the court find the search was incident to the arrest? Yes, sir. They found that the entire search was incident to the arrest. Some of the items were discovered that all the arrests were made. The record is not entirely clear on that, and in the dissenting opinion in the Fourth Circuit, Judge Bryan's opinion, he expresses the opinion that the evidence is clear that the clothing was found before the man was arrested. I do not believe that it is clear. We cannot tell from what the officers remember, and we tried to establish... Did the district court find that? No, sir. I believe they found that the items had been found shortly after the arrest or almost contemporaneously. The officer who was in the basement had first, and everybody agrees to this, even Mr. Hayden has stated, did come upstairs and say, I find nobody in the basement. It was at this point that they knew that Mr. Hayden was the only colored male in the house and arrested him. The officer indicated, though he could not be totally sure, that he had not found the clothing at that time, but he wasn't totally sure. He may have at that time come upstairs with the clothing, but he does not remember, and there was no... At least the seizure. Yes, sir. And all of the... Mr. Hayden did know, and he so testified, what items were found by the time he left the house. So they were found either contemporaneously with the arrest or immediately before while they were still searching for the man. They were discovered, that is, immediately before while they were searching for the man, but certainly were seized and taken after he was arrested. Are they searching for the man who arrested? Yes, sir. They entered the house for the express purpose. They announced immediately upon entering the house to Mrs. Hayden, and even she admits this, we believe a robber ran in here. And this was stated as soon as they came in, they were looking for the robber they intended to arrest him. I may point out, they did not know and had no way of knowing whether Mr. Hayden, or the man who ran in, belonged in that house. And if he did not belong in that house, the people in that house were in danger, and I am sure that this was in the minds of the policemen at the same time. They knew that a man had run into that house. They did not know he was the occupant of the house. They did not for sure know when Mrs. Hayden came to the door that perhaps someone had a gun trained on her at that time. This court, in I believe a very recent civil case, has had to deal with the desperate hours situation, and the police had no way of knowing that this wasn't a similar type situation. They wanted to go in there and to arrest the man who had committed the felony, and if he was not the occupant of the house, there was certainly even greater reason to go in because the people in that house then were also in danger. The primary point presented in our petition for rid of certiorari and the point on which the... What would be your position if they hadn't seized this property as they went in to arrest him and why they wanted him? Excuse me, sir, I didn't... What would be your position if you say now that the district court held one way, what would it be held the other way, that the property was seized before they arrested him? What would be your position with reference to seizing the property if they went in after the man and were chasing him and found this property? My position, Mr. Justice Black, would be that this would also be proper because their entire purpose in going in was to make the arrest. In the course of making the arrest, they knew that they were looking for a man who had a weapon. They knew they had to protect themselves and they knew they had to protect the people that were in the house. In the course of making the search, I do not believe that you can define it that close as long as their purpose in going in was clearly to arrest and not to make the search. The entire thing at that point was to arrest the man, prevent him from escaping, prevent him from utilizing the weapon they knew he had. So that if, in fact, and I think all of the district court and all the five members of the Circuit Court of Appeals agree that it really didn't make any difference if technically or actually the clothing was found immediately before they arrested him or immediately after as long as their entire purpose was not going in to make the search. Their purpose was to make the arrest. As part of that arrest, they had to be sure that they disarmed this man. And certainly at the time the officer went to the basement, he did not know where the gun was. And I think, therefore, it would be proper under any circumstance and therefore would not be at issue here. But the primary point which we have raised and upon which the Solicitor General has filed a brief amicus is whether the majority of the Fourth Circuit incorrectly held that the clothing was not subject to seizure. Here, the Fourth Circuit found that there was a rule based upon the decisions of this court which prevented the seizure of extremely relevant evidence reasonably obtained and the Fourth Circuit held that this was a rule of constitutional dimensions and merely because these items which were relevant could not technically be classed as means of committing the crime, instrumentality of the crime, or contraband. All of the courts who have dealt with it have dealt with it on that basis, sir. The guns certainly were means of committing the crime. No one has ever made an issue of the ammunition that fit in the gun, but I believe that this certainly would also be part of the means of committing the crime. The only other items would be the clothing, sir. The question points up one of the difficulties of this mere evidence rule, doesn't it? That is, what is mere evidence and what isn't? What is fruits or instrumentalities or various other phrases that have been used? Mr. Stewart, I have tried to not utilize the expression mere evidence. You call it the quote, rule, unquote. Yes, sir. I feel that saying that it is mere really... I read you, brief. What do you want us to do with Gulen? I do not believe for the state's purpose... Distinguish it out of existence or overrule it? Mr. Justice Douglas, I do not believe that for the state's purpose, you have to overrule it. I think you could find that Gulen does not present a rule which is of constitutional dimensions which is applicable to the states and under Kerr, that the states could set up their own workable rules for seizures here. I do believe, honestly, though, that Gulen to the extent that it supports the so-called mere evidence rule should to that extent be overruled. Of course, Gulen only... And restricted to what? Letters? That could be done, sir, but my... How about why can't? My own belief is that... Excuse me. My own belief is that Gulen should be totally overruled even as to documentary evidence because if it is found in the type of search that we had here, I do not believe that there is any right of the accused that is worthy of protection that is upheld by saying that where the police are in the house as part of a reasonable arrest and reasonable search, and while they're searching for the items which can be taken, like the guns and like the money, which are classed as means or fruits or contraband, if they happen to also find documentary evidence which is just as damning towards conviction or towards showing that this is the man, I see no reason because there's no further invasion of privacy. No reason would be the Fourth Amendment. But the Fourth Amendment, sir, as I understand it, would be to prevent an unreasonable search. Under this circumstance, under this type of factual situation, I do not believe that it can be said that the search would be unreasonable. Well, then you would want us to overrule Boyd as well as Doolett. Boyd is a different situation, sir, in that in Boyd, I believe you do have clearly the Fifth Amendment proposition set forth. There, it was a compulsion to produce, and you do have documentary evidence, so I believe the privilege against self-incrimination in the Fifth Amendment is the primary thing behind Boyd. Boyd would not have to be overruled. Well, this is a coercive situation. We're not, this man isn't there by invitation. But he is there having the full right to be in hot pursuit, having the full right to arrest. any burden on Mr. Hayden, any violation of Mr. Hayden's rights, any indignity Mr. Hayden is supposed to have suffered, is brought about by the fact that the police have the right to be there, and in fact the duty and obligation to be there, to arrest him. In the factual situation here, I would say that there would be no reason to exclude any type of evidence that is found in that search. But I do believe that this court could decide in our favor without overruling even gulad as to documentary evidence. The court could say that only as to clothing or these type of items, which are certainly even very close to being considered instrumentalities of the crime, that could decide in our favor without overruling gulad completely. But you asked me what my belief was on it, sir, and I honestly believe that the rights of the accused will be protected and the police will be better able to utilize what this court has asked for, scientific investigation, if gulad to the entire extent would be overruled, where there is a search like this incident to a legal arrest. I noticed, since I've tried to save a little bit of time for rebuttal, that I do not have too much time remaining. I did want to say that we... The Socialist General, as I like this, does the full length of the legal arrest? Yes, sir, I believe he does. I would like to say that I do believe that the reasoning in the Schmerber case, not just the holding, but the entire reasoning in the Schmerber case, supports us completely. I think that if we say that the blood in Schmerber was, if we want to use the expression mere evidence, I think it certainly was. It was wanted only for evidentiary purposes, and yet it was found that the search and seizure, which this court found the taking of the blood was a search and seizure, was reasonable. If the taking of the blood in Schmerber was a reasonable search under the Fourth Amendment, I think that this is an A4 sure-eye case, that this certainly was a reasonable search and seizure under the Fourth Amendment and should not in any way be restricted. Mr. Turnbull has once again brought up the question of exploratory search. I did not believe that that was still in the case. All the courts below have found that the search was in no way exploratory. I don't believe that the search was. I think it was far less extensive than the search in Harris. Harrison and Harris, they went in with an arrest warrant, knew what they wanted, but yet they didn't get a search warrant. Here the police had no time in which to get a search warrant. If that man was in the house, was not the occupant of the house, they had to be in there quickly to arrest him and to protect the people in the house. They went in and as part of the search for the guns and the money, found the clothing. there certainly was nothing exploratory here. This is not the vehicle to re-examine Harris, even if this court at some time decides to re-examine Harris. I also believe that the decision of this court in Linkletter would show that even if Harris were to be at some future time overruled, it would not be overruled retrospectively or retroactively, and therefore, in a state conviction such as this, it would not at this time say that Mr. Hayden's search was exploratory and therefore bad. So I do not think that the exploratory point is well taken here, even if it was adequately preserved here. It was not mentioned in the brief in opposition to our petition for certiorari. In fact, this might be a hot pursuit to affect the situation in any also? I think it clearly does. I think that where the police have come in in this type of situation where they have to go in immediately, that they have to search everything that is under the man's control. It was pointed out that the clothing was found in the basement and that he was found on the second floor. But suppose, for example, he had broken away from the police. This is a possibility. It can happen if they had grabbed the gun beforehand. They're better able to protect themselves and the other people in the house. And certainly, I think it is true also, that when they went to the basement, they were looking for the man. I won't go into the point... Oh, they'd seen him in the basement as they were pursuing him, hardly. So these clothes off and put him in there. Would there have been any difference? I'm afraid according to the majority of the Fourth Circuit, they would say that there would not be any difference, that it would still be mere evidence. And this is where I think the rule is shown to be so illogical. Where the man takes these clothes off in order to avoid the detection, and I think the police could testify to the fact that the clothing was in the washing machine in that condition, and if they can testify to it, I see no reason why they shouldn't be able to take it. I'm afraid if they testified to it and didn't bring it in, we might have someone say we were suppressing the evidence. And I think... The Fourth Circuit would exclude the testimony, too. I'm not entirely... Because you only got it according to them by an illegal search. No, they found the search, Mr. Justice Wright, I believe they found the search to have been legal. It was only the seizure that was illegal, so I think even the majority of the Fourth Circuit would have found that the police could have testified to the fact that the clothing was in the washing machine. They did not find the search. You may search for mere evidence, according to the Fourth Circuit. I believe their decision fairly appraised would be that, that you may search, or if you happen in a legal search to see mere evidence, you can testify about it, but you can't take it. And I believe there, too, we point up the fact that the rule is illogical and doesn't merit this Court to continue it. The majority of the Fourth Circuit did feel that this Court should reexamine and reinterpret the rule, and I think they were right in that. I will not go into my last point because it's something I just preserved. I feel that I would hope that this Court would decide in our favor on the so-called mere evidence point, and therefore our other point would be moot. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Spitzer. Mr. Chief Justice, Your Honors, I'd like to begin by stating the interest of the United States in this case. As the Court has already heard, the Fourth Circuit felt itself constrained by the Goulet decision to hold that an object which has evidentiary value, and evidentiary value without some added factor, is not subject to a search and seizure. The Court has said it only becomes subject to the seizure if it also qualifies as an instrumentality of the crime, as a fruit of the crime, or as contraband. And as you have heard, concluding that the robber's clothing in this case was not an instrumentality of the crime, the Court concluded that the Maryland authorities had not been free to seize that clothing, to show it to the eyewitnesses to the crime, or to offer their testimony associating the items of clothing with the person of the defendant as they had seen him at the scene of the crime. Judge Sobeloff, excuse me. I misunderstood Mr. Goldstein, and I've forgotten. Did the Fourth Circuit say that there may be no testimony about the clothing in this case? I think the opinion rests on the fact that the seizure and the introduction of the clothing was bad. And I don't know that one, I hesitate to say from my reading of the opinion, whether the Court would conclude that testimony would be forbidden, that is, testimony by the police officers as to what they saw. The basis of the decision is clearly that it was error to introduce the clothing itself into evidence. So you're suggesting that it's open in this case as to whether testimony by the police to the effect that they saw the clothing would be a reversible error. I'm suggesting that the Court of Appeals never reached that question. Now, the Fourth Circuit, Judge Sobeloff's opinion, recognized that the Gouled rule has been very widely criticized, even by those whom he termed staunch defenders of individual liberty. He said, however, that as a subordinate judge, he felt obliged to follow it here. Of course, that would be true of a lot of our decisions. His obligation to follow them, indeed so. Well, I mean, in fact, they're criticized, doesn't it? No, he was pointing out that they had been criticized by those who urged a broad view of the protections of the Fourth Amendment as being unrelated to the purposes which that amendment should serve. Now, this issue does arise, I wish to point out with some frequency in federal cases also, because typically an officer makes a lawful arrest, he makes some certain incident to that arrest, and he discovers some telltale item of evidence. more often than not, that item is ultimately admitted. Unsympathetic to the Guled line of distinction, the lower courts have gone very far in expanding the concept of instrumentality of the crime. Indeed, lower courts, in a number of instances, have held that clothing which is worn by a robber or a burglar is. is an instrumentality of the crime because the absence of clothing would obviously hinder the offender in its perpetration. Well, that might be true certainly of shoes. The court, I'm not urging that that kind of an artificial distinction is the ideal way to dispose of this issue. Your ideal way is to reverse Gulen. yes, I think that the test under the Fourth Amendment should not be based upon a determination whether the item is mere evidence, but rather the Fourth Amendment should be frankly applied by a determination whether there was probable cause, whether the requirement of specificity was met, and whether the search was in all of its attendant circumstances a reasonable one. I am not urging for a moment, Your Honor, that because an item is evidence, it is invariably subject to seizure. I am arguing that because it is evidence, it should not be immune from seizure. We are not for a moment challenging the precepts of the Boyd case, for example. We recognize that private papers by their ... Boyd, of course, involved something like a subpoena, I suppose. what we are talking about here is, suppose Boyd had involved only a search warrant, not a subpoena. Wasn't it a subpoena? Boyd involved a subpoena, and there was that fifth amendment objection as well. Suppose it had been a search warrant. Would you still think Boyd was soundly decided? Boyd's assumption, as I read the opinion, was that private papers were involved there. Now, it might have been argued that they were not truly private papers, but they were commercial papers. I think the court assumed that they were. We assume that private papers are entitled to a special measure of protection. Under the Fourth? Under the Fourth and Fifth Amendments, and one of the reasons certainly is that the Fifth Amendment immediately becomes strongly implicated, as Boyd itself said. You don't want to gool it, because there was a warrant in Guled, wasn't there? Was there being a warrant in the subpoena? There were two parts to Guled, Your Honor, will recall. The part we're talking about here, which relied on the mere evidence rule, that involved a search under a warrant. And that warrant was an element of compulsion, like a subpoena, isn't it? Not in the same sense as a subpoena. One of the problems, as I see it in Boyd, and this was the basis of the concurring opinion, I believe, was that when one makes a return to a subpoena, one authenticates. One says, this is the document called for by the subpoena. That itself might be a violation of the Fifth Amendment. Whereas if someone comes in with a warrant and takes an item, which is not a test, let's assume it's not testimonial in any sense, it's not a paper, it's a tangible object, as here a piece of clothing. In such a circumstance, I don't think one has the Fifth Amendment problems that were present in the case of private terrorism. That was a coercive, we held a coercive situation? I think that a warrant does involve coercion, certainly. The person has no power to prevent the officers lawfully acting under a warrant from taking that, which is embraced by the warrant. I think that, however, is a distinct question from testimonial compulsion. And I think this case does not implicate the Fifth Amendment problems. Well, I think it does not implicate it by a taking of clothing as distinguished from a taking of private papers. Indeed, it seems to me that this case is certainly out for your eye from a case like Schmerber, because in Schmerber there was active participation, the necessity either of active participation by the offender or the necessity of overcoming his will before the blood sample could be taken from him. In Schmerber there was certainly intrusion into a very private area, the human body, and it seems to me that a case like this is a much easier case. It seems to me also, since we're talking about clothing here, that if any tangible object is non-communicative or non-testimonial in its character, then certainly the tangible objects with which we're dealing here fall into that category. I suppose that's as far as you have to go to decide this case. But I wasn't clear whether under your belief you were urging on us, that even if, assuming now that a search warrant is coercive, is compulsive, even if that does not, by reason of any fifth amendment over town, bar it choose to get physical evidence. You're not asking us to say, are you, that nor would it bar it choose to get evidence which indeed is testimonial, as I put it to you before a confession? No, I'm not, I'm addressing myself to tangible objects. Well, this case does involve a fairly broad category, because there are numerous cases in which the police sees objects. in the typical narcotics case, which we see so many. Where was the clothing? Pardon? Where was the clothing? It was in two places, your honor. The policeman who went down to the basement looking for the offender picked up the lid of the washing machine, and he saw the trousers and the jacket. The policeman who went upstairs and arrested the man whom they found in bed upstairs, lifted up the mattress, and they found the cap which corresponded to the description they had received, together with a clip of ammunition under the mattress. So the clothing was located in two places. Now you'd say that we'd have to trim Gouled over it or something? Insofar as Gouled enunciated the rule, that no item which is so-called mere evidence may be the subject of a seizure. I think you would have to depart from Gouled. I thought Gouled depended upon the earlier case of Boyd. He cited Boyd. He was all papers, he was all the search warrant. It did, but Gouled didn't rest on that. It said that even if it had been, well it had said that if it had been shown that these papers were instrumentalities of the crime, they could have been seized. Suppose this clothing was marijuana, or a brick of the... I'm sorry, I didn't catch you. Suppose this clothing was a brick of some narcotics or something. would that be violate 4th Emma?
